transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-17
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Singh (Polaris Vital), Evan Roberts (Platform), Lina Park (Security), Tom Alvarez (Product)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on Polaris Vital's path to first token using Redwood's PLG quickstart, options between Hosted/Dedicated/Private, and security requirements for a pilot. Customer is evaluating tradeoffs between latency and cost and has regulatory concerns around PHI. They requested pricing, SOC2/ISO excerpts, and a short benchmark with their prompts.

Topics: quickstart flow, free credits, time-to-first-token, hosted vs dedicated vs private, VPC/KMS, SOC two/ISO, quantization and latency tradeoffs, batching/caching, rollout/canary plan, pilot success criteria

Transcript body:
00:00:05 Jamie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jamie Carter, AE on the account, and I have Priya, our solutions engineer with me. How's everyone doing?
00:00:12 Dr. Maya Singh (Polaris): Doing good, thanks. Quick call — a few folks on our side. I'm Maya, head of ML. Evan's platform, Lina security, Tom product.
00:00:20 Jamie: Awesome. We'll move through a short agenda: quickstart and credits, hosted vs dedicated vs private options, security checklist, then next steps. Priya will handle the tech details. Does that work?
00:00:28 Evan: Yep, works for us.
00:00:35 Priya (Redwood SE): Cool, I'll start with quickstart. The PLG flow is usually sign up, get free credits, run a hello world to get time-to-first-token in minutes. We have SDKs and an API, and a sample notebook that preloads a prompt set. The important bit is our console shows token break down so you can track cost.
00:00:56 Tom (Polaris): When you say "time-to-first-token", what do you mean exactly? Like in production or dev sandbox?
00:01:02 Priya: Mostly sandbox — get a token from the hosted API within a few minutes post signup. For production we'd set up either dedicated or private depending on needs, but the quickstart is hosted and intended for rapid validation.
00:01:15 Dr. Maya: We have PHI involved; that's our main regulatory worry. We need to understand data retention and K-M-S integration. We can't have logs stored in a shared tenant for long.
00:01:27 Jamie: Totally. For pilots we usually set data retention policies and can route to dedicated tenancy. We also have Private deploy with customer-managed control plane for stricter needs. Priya, can you run through the differences?
00:01:40 Priya: Sure. Hosted: fastest onboarding, free credits, fully managed, best for dev/eval. Dedicated: reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and isolation — think of it as your tenant on shared infra but dedicated capacity. Private: VPC or on-prem bundle, customer-managed networking, KMS/HSM integration, full audit logs. Note sometimes folks call KV cache the K-V cash in transcripts, but it's KV cache — that's important for latency.
00:02:05 Evan: For our expected traffic — bursts up to 120 rps during sync windows — what does dedicated look like?
00:02:12 Priya: You can size reserved capacity to handle your 95th percentile. We recommend a mix: a baseline dedicated capacity plus hosted overflow for bursts if you need elastic burst capacity. Routing policy can failover to hosted variants if capacity is constrained.
00:02:30 Lina (Security): On encryption — can we manage keys? We want HSM-backed KMS and not share keys. Also audit logs need to land in our SIEM.
00:02:39 Jamie: Yes, Private supports HSM KMS and audit logs; Dedicated has integrations with customer KMS in many cases. We'll send the KMS guide.
00:02:46 Dr. Maya: Another thing — model quality. We test with long clinical notes — average 1,100 tokens per request. Latency is critical; we can't wait 2–3 seconds per token. How do you optimize?
00:02:58 Priya: Two levers — model variant/quantization and runtime optimizations. Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles; continuous batching and KV caching reduce per-token compute. For long sequences, kernel selection matters. We can run a small benchmark with your prompt set to show token throughput and latency tradeoffs.
00:03:18 Tom: Is quantization available in hosted? I recall some vendors don't allow lower-precision models in shared infra.
00:03:24 Priya: We have quant variants in hosted catalog for certain models, but for aggressive quantization customers prefer Dedicated/Private because it gives more predictable performance. We can show measured deltas during the benchmark.
00:03:36 Evan: Ok. On the integration side, we mostly use Kubernetes + internal model cache. We may want to colocate at edge. Does Redwood support regional routing and private peering?
00:03:46 Jamie: Yes — for dedicated and private we can set region preferences and peering. Hosted supports region selection for lower latency from supported cloud regions.
00:03:55 Lina: Regarding compliance — do you have SOC two and ISO2 seven — is that public?
00:04:03 Jamie: Yes, SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 summaries are available; we'll send the certs and a 1–pager on audit scope. Also we can share a redacted penetration test report.
00:04:14 Dr. Maya: Great. For a pilot we'd prefer a 4-week PoC: integrate with dev, run benchmarks, evaluate latency/cost, and confirm security posture. What does Redwood typically charge for pilots?
00:04:25 Jamie: For PLG you can run freely with credits; for a pilot that needs dedicated capacity we have short-term reserved pricing or trial credits for dedicated for qualifying customers. We'll put together a pilot proposal with pricing ranges.
00:04:36 Evan: About cost controls — can we get token-level cost alerts and throttles? We need to avoid runaway bills during test failures.
00:04:44 Priya: Yep, the Console has token-level cost breakdowns, budget alerts, rate limiting and per-route quotas. We can set API keys with per-key quotas for the pilot.
00:04:55 Tom: One minor but practical thing — if we move to Private later, what's the typical lift? How many weeks?
00:05:02 Priya: Private VPC with managed control plane is usually 4–8 weeks depending on networking approvals; on-prem longer. We have a checklist that speeds that up — network ranges, firewall rules, KMS certs, storage endpoints. We'll share that.
00:05:15 Dr. Maya: Who owns model updates and rollouts? We need canary testing and rollback in case of regressions.
00:05:21 Priya: Rollouts are managed via the Console; you can do canary, A/B, and automatic fallback policies. You can pin versions per route. We also have quality monitors to catch regressions against prompt sets.
00:05:33 Lina: How do you handle logging for PHI? Do you have an option to redact sensitive entities or keep logs ephemeral?
00:05:40 Jamie: For PHI, we usually recommend no logs persisted in shared hosted for regulated data — use Dedicated with short retention or Private. We also provide configurable redaction and a policy to avoid storing raw prompts.
00:05:51 Evan: Any blockers for us to try the quickstart today? We just want to validate the dev flow and run a unit of tests.
00:05:58 Jamie: No blockers — I'll send the quickstart link and free credits. You can get a token and call in minutes. Priya, anything to add?
00:06:05 Priya: I'll include a small notebook that shows time-to-first-token, how to set up an SDK key with quotas, and how to run a sample benchmark script. Also I'll include a sample prompt set tailored to long clinical notes.
00:06:15 Dr. Maya: Nice. A couple of clarifying Qs — what metrics do you surface in the Console? We need per-route p50/p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, and token counts.
00:06:25 Priya: All of those, plus per-model breakdown, token-type breakdown, and per-key usage. We also support tracing hooks for distributed tracing.
00:06:34 Tom: We sometimes run into transcription errors when we import calls for QA — unrelated, but—
00:06:39 Jamie: (laughs) noted.
00:06:45 Lina: On the security questionnaire we sent, there were a few items about onboarding flow and admin RBAC. Can Redwood integrate with our SSO (SAML/Okta)?
00:06:53 Jamie: Yes, SSO with SAML and SCIM provisioning and RBAC is supported. We'll attach an Okta guide.
00:07:01 Dr. Maya: If we run the benchmark and results look good, what's the path to production? Pilot -> Dedicated reservation -> Private if needed?
00:07:08 Priya: Exactly. Most customers start hosted for dev with free credits, run a pilot on dedicated for predictable latency and cost, then consider Private for strict compliance or residency.
00:07:18 Evan: For the benchmark, Priya, can you simulate our 1,100 token average? And show batching behavior?
00:07:25 Priya: Yep. We'll run a bench that matches your seq length distribution and traffic profile. We'll show p50/p95 and cost per token under different configs and quant levels.
00:07:33 Tom: Any customer references in healthcare? Would be helpful.
00:07:37 Jamie: We have a couple of health customers we can introduce — I'll check with marketing about reference rules and share anonymized case studies.
00:07:45 Dr. Maya: Perfect. Let's lock down a date for the benchmark. How about Jan 26? That gives us time to assemble prompt set.
00:07:52 Priya: Jan 26 works on our side. We'll book a 2-3 hour window for test runs.
00:07:58 Jamie: Great. I'll follow up with an invite and materials. Any other questions?
00:08:04 Lina: One last — when do credits expire? We want to ensure we can use them on our schedule.
00:08:10 Jamie: Free credits are usually valid for 90 days from issue; for pilots we can extend or issue dedicated trial credits. We'll note that in the follow-up.
00:08:17 Tom: Sounds good.
00:08:22 (brief cross-talk while shares exchanged)
00:09:05 Jamie: Quick recap — we'll send: quickstart link + free credits, SOC2/ISO PDFs and KMS integration guide, pricing ranges for pilot/dedicated, and a benchmarking plan for Jan 26. Action owners: Jamie sends pricing and references, Priya runs bench plan, Lina provides security Qs, Evan provides traffic profile.
00:09:35 Dr. Maya: Good summary. Thanks, everyone.
00:09:40 Jamie: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.

End of transcript.
